summary: Defines an optional extension to RELOAD, a peer-to-peer signaling protocol, that supports direct response routing. This shortens the path of responses and reduces the load on intermediate peers.

plainLanguage.summary: In a game of passing notes, the answer can go straight back to the asker instead of through everyone. That saves the helpers in the middle from extra work.

questions: what is reload direct response routing
subtitle: Letting RELOAD responses go straight back to the requester instead of retracing the request's path.

tldr.problem: RELOAD recommends symmetric recursive routing, where each response retraces the request's path through every intermediate peer. That adds bandwidth, CPU and battery load on those peers.
tldr.mechanism: The sending peer includes a new extensive_routing_mode forwarding option with its own transport address, and the destination peer sends the response directly to that address. SRR remains the fallback.
tldr.outcome: In suitable networks, such as closed or managed ones, responses take a shorter route and intermediate peers do less work. DRR is optional, and the RFC says it SHOULD NOT be used in the open Internet.

today: RFC 7263 is a Proposed Standard from June 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends RFC 6940, with relay peer routing covered in RFC 7264.

sections.title: Why Add Direct Response Routing
sections.content:
The REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD) protocol, RFC 6940, recommends symmetric recursive routing (SRR) and discusses two other options in its Appendix A: direct response routing (DRR) and relay peer routing (RPR). This RFC turns DRR into a standalone extension to RELOAD. RPR is covered separately in RFC 7264.

DRR can reduce CPU and link bandwidth load on intermediate peers. In a closed network where every peer is in the same address realm it performs better than SRR, and in other scenarios a combination of DRR and SRR is more likely to help than SRR alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes there is a shortcut for the answer to take. This document teaches the network how to use the shortcut safely.

sections.title: SRR Versus DRR
sections.content:
RELOAD is a simple request-response protocol. In the RFC's illustrations, peer A sends a request to the peer responsible for a Resource-ID k, which is peer X, through intermediate peers B, C and D.

With SRR, each intermediate peer adds the peer it got the request from to the Via List. Peer X then builds a Destination List from the Via List and the response retraces the path. This works in any situation, especially with NATs or firewalls, but the message takes several hops back, which increases bandwidth use and CPU or battery load on multiple peers.

With DRR, the request travels the same way, but peer X sends the response directly to peer A's local transport address. Intermediate peers never see the response. If there are no NATs, or the NAT implements endpoint-independent filtering, this is the optimal technique.

The RFC names two scenarios: managed or closed P2P systems on private networks, and mobile or wireless deployments where DRR may reduce radio battery usage and bandwidth by the intermediate peers.
sections.plainLanguage: SRR is passing the answer back through every kid in the line. DRR is the answerer walking it to you. The long way always works, and the short way works when nothing blocks the path.

sections.title: Using DRR and SRR Together
sections.content:
DRR is not intended to replace SRR. Per RFC 6940, SRR MUST be supported, and an overlay MAY be configured to use alternative routing algorithms, selected even per message. All peers MUST be able to process SRR requests and MAY support DRR.

A joining node should read its preferred routing mode from the overlay configuration file. This RFC adds a route-mode element inside each configuration element, using the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:route-mode. The mode can be DRR or RPR and, if given, is the preferred mode.

In a private overlay where all peers can reach each other, peers MAY send most transactions with DRR. DRR SHOULD NOT be used in the open Internet, or when the administrator lacks enough information about the topology.

A peer can start with DRR and track its success rate. If DRR fails, it switches to SRR. A simple policy is to switch to SRR for all connections. A finer policy keeps a list of unreachable peers and uses only SRR for them. The RFC recommends deciding from overall DRR success statistics, not per connection, which should be an application decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The network starts with the shortcut if the rules say so. If the shortcut does not work, it goes back to the long way, and it remembers which shortcuts failed.

sections.title: The Forwarding Option and Flag
sections.content:
RELOAD is extensible through forwarding options. This RFC defines two additions.

The IGNORE-STATE-KEEPING flag, value 0x08, tells intermediate peers they may skip keeping state. SRR lets intermediate peers keep state, for example for hop-by-hop retransmission. With DRR, the response does not come back through them, so that state would only be cleared on expiry. When the flag is set, a peer that is not the destination SHOULD forward the message with the full Via List and SHOULD NOT maintain any internal state.

The extensive_routing_mode option carries an ExtensiveRoutingModeOption structure with four fields: routemode (0 is reserved and DRR is 1), transport (the transport type for the response), ipaddressport (the address the destination peer should send to), and destinations (the sending peer itself; for DRR this holds only the sender's Node-ID).
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a small note saying 'send the answer to this address' and another saying 'you in the middle, do not bother remembering this one'.

sections.title: Sending Requests and Responses
sections.content:
To use DRR, the sending peer MUST set the IGNORE-STATE-KEEPING flag and MUST include a ForwardingOption of type extensive_routing_mode. Inside, routemode is 0x01, transport is set as appropriate, ipaddressport is the peer's associated transport address, and the destination structure holds exactly one value of type node with the sender's own values.

The destination peer checks the forwarding options. If it does not understand extensive_routing_mode, it MUST try to return an Error_Unknown_Extension response using SRR. If the mode is DRR, it MUST build a Destination List with a single entry, the requester's Node-ID from the Via List, and send the response to the address in ipaddressport. If DRR is set but there is not exactly one destination, it MUST try to return Error_Unknown_Extension using SRR.

If the destination peer receives a retransmit with SRR preference for the message it is answering, it SHOULD abort the DRR response and use SRR. The sending peer SHOULD note whether DRR worked, and if no response arrives before the timeout, it SHOULD resend the request using SRR.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker writes their own address on the request. The answerer sends the reply there, and if it never arrives, the asker just asks again the long way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The normative security recommendations of Section 13 of RFC 6940 apply. DRR conforms to Section 13.6 of RFC 6940, which covers routing security. Because the DRR option gives information about the route back to the source, the entire DRR routing message MUST be digitally signed and sent over a protected channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the note says where to send the answer, it has to be signed and sent safely so nobody can change the address.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Appendices
sections.content:
IANA added a RELOAD Forwarding Option with code 2 and name extensive_routing_mode to the registry defined in RFC 6940. It also registered the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:route-mode in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant contact.

Two informative appendices help peers decide whether to try DRR. Appendix A describes how a peer can find candidate addresses using STUN, UPnP-IGD or NAT-PMP, and test whether an address is publicly reachable by asking an overlay peer with no direct connection to it to send an unsolicited response. It notes that there is no foolproof way to determine public reachability other than out-of-band mechanisms. Appendix B compares the cost of SRR and DRR in closed and open networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list got a new entry so nobody else reuses the same label. The extra pages explain how to check whether the shortcut will work.
